In 1932, Australia sent soldiers with machine guns to fight a war against birds. And the birds won.
After World War One, thousands of veterans were given land in Western Australia to grow wheat.
Then about twenty thousand emus showed up.
Emus are huge, they can run around fifty kilometers an hour, and they love wheat.
The farmers asked for help, and the army sent Major Meredith, two soldiers, two machine guns, and ten thousand rounds of ammunition.
On day one, the emus saw the guns, split up, and ran.
So the soldiers set up an ambush near a dam, with about a thousand emus walking straight toward them.
They opened fire. After only a few birds fell, the gun jammed.
They even mounted a machine gun on a truck. But the truck was too slow, and the ride was so bumpy nobody could aim.
After a week, the army pulled out.
They came back for a second try, and claimed almost a thousand birds, at about ten bullets per emu.
But the emus were still there.
Meredith said that with the bullet-carrying capacity of these birds, an army could face anyone in the world.
In the end, farmers had better luck with bounties and fences.
And the emus? Still running around Australia today.
